Title: Week 62: Emergency As Standing Policy
Content:
War in Iran, a weaponized shutdown at home, and a coordinated squeeze on voting and citizenship turned crisis into the default mode of governance.

The sixty-second week of Trump’s second term unfolded as a study in layered strain rather than a single break. War abroad, shutdown at home, and a grinding fight over who counts as a voter and a citizen all moved forward at once. Each domain had its own logic and actors, yet together they described a government that treated crisis as a standing condition and used it to redraw the lines of power. The pattern was not new. What changed was the confidence with which it was applied and the breadth of systems it now touched.

At the close of the previous period, the Democracy Clock stood at 8:13 p.m. By the end of this week, it remained at 8:13 p.m., a net change of zero minutes. The stillness in the measure did not reflect calm. It reflected offsetting forces: deepening unilateral war-making, voter restriction, and stratified citizenship on one side, and pockets of institutional and civic resistance on the other. The balance held, but only because courts, states, and civil society absorbed more strain to counter moves that, left unchecked, would have pushed the clock forward.

The week’s central axis was the Iran war, now plainly an executive project. Early in the period, reports surfaced that the administration had weighed an assault on Iran’s Kharg Island and prepared thousands of Marines for deployment. These were not contingency plans in a distant file. They were active options, readied by the Pentagon under presidential direction. Trump then publicly threatened to “obliterate” Iranian power plants if the Strait of Hormuz was not reopened, signaling a willingness to target civilian infrastructure in service of coercive aims. The language was blunt. The chain of authority was short.

As the days passed, the president announced and then extended pauses of planned bombing campaigns, claiming negotiations with Tehran that Iranian officials denied. Each pause and claimed breakthrough moved markets and shaped public expectations, yet none passed through the formal channels that usually accompany war and peace. Behind the announcements, the Pentagon deployed and prepared to deploy large Army and Marine units to the region, deepening U.S. entanglement without new authorization. By week’s end, Trump described the Iran campaign as a “military operation” and a success, even as he acknowledged that Congress had not approved it. Hostilities of that scale were treated as a matter of presidential discretion.

Foreign influence threaded through these decisions. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman lobbied Trump to continue and expand the war, pressing for strikes that looked less like self-defense and more like regime change. Israeli leaders also urged escalation. At the same time, Saudi funds flowed into Jared Kushner’s investment firm and a Trump-branded development, tying the president’s family finances to a monarchy with a direct stake in Iran’s fate. When Trump launched strikes on Iran at the urging of these leaders, without an imminent threat finding, it underscored how personal relationships and foreign interests could shape U.S. war decisions more than institutional checks.

Congress appeared in this story mostly as a frustrated observer. Republican leaders refused to hold hearings that might scrutinize the war’s justification, choosing instead to back the president and avoid public oversight. Senate Democrats tried to require congressional authorization for continued operations, but their efforts failed. Members in both chambers sought more detailed briefings on strategy, costs, and objectives, only to receive vague presentations that left nearly $30 billion in war spending and major shifts in alliance priorities largely unexplained. The constitutional allocation of war powers remained on paper. In practice, the presidency acted first and informed later, if at all.

The conflict in the Gulf was not only a military affair. It became an economic shock tool. Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz and imposed tolls on ships, disrupting a key route for global oil and liquefied natural gas. Iraq declared force majeure on foreign-operated oilfields, unable to fulfill contracts because exports could not move. Fuel shortages and price spikes rippled outward. In parts of Asia, governments ordered work-from-home arrangements, shortened workweeks, and early university closures to conserve fuel. A distant strait became a lever on daily life for millions.

The Trump administration responded by easing sanctions in ways that blended war policy with market management. Treasury and the White House lifted or waived sanctions on roughly 140 million barrels of Iranian oil already at sea, allowing it to reach market to lower prices even as U.S. forces fought Iranian targets. Sanctions on Belarus were relaxed to secure fertilizer imports, trading away human-rights leverage for short-term economic relief. At home, the U.S. Postal Service prepared an eight percent fuel surcharge on packages, passing war-driven costs to households and small businesses. The executive branch thus used sanctions relief and emergency surcharges to manage the fallout, with little visible legislative input, while the burdens of geopolitical risk settled on ordinary people.

If war abroad showed one face of emergency governance, the prolonged shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security showed another. For weeks, Congress failed to agree on DHS funding. Seven Senate votes collapsed amid disputes over immigration enforcement and voting provisions. A Senate-passed package that omitted ICE funding stalled when House Republicans refused to take it up, preferring alternative plans that preserved leverage. The result was a partially unfunded security department, unpaid workers, and mounting operational strain.

Into that vacuum stepped the president and his preferred enforcement arm. Trump threatened to deploy Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents to airports to backfill unpaid Transportation Security Administration staff, then followed through. ICE officers in tactical gear appeared in civilian terminals, performing screening functions that had long been the domain of specialized, non-immigration personnel. The move turned immigration enforcement into a visible political tool in everyday public space, blurring the line between border policing and routine security to pressure Congress. Hearings in the House documented the human cost: TSA workers struggling without pay, ICE transfers to airports, and poor conditions in detention centers. The stories were concrete. The strain was visible.

As the shutdown dragged on, Trump issued an executive order directing DHS to pay TSA agents despite the funding lapse. The order relieved immediate hardship but did so by improvising around appropriations rules, reinforcing the idea that the president could patch over legislative failure with ad hoc decrees. At the same time, the Senate confirmed a loyal Trump ally, Markwayne Mullin, as Secretary of Homeland Security, placing a political confidant atop a vast security bureaucracy in the midst of a shutdown and immigration crackdown. Civil service roles that had once rested on professional norms were now shaped by partisan loyalty and emergency workarounds.

The fight over who would be screened at airports and who would be paid for it ran parallel to a broader campaign over who would be allowed to vote. Trump and his allies pushed the SAVE America Act, which tied DHS funding to strict proof-of-citizenship requirements and new voter ID rules. Senate Republicans explored using budget reconciliation to finance ICE and embed SAVE provisions, a way to bypass the filibuster and enact contentious voting changes with a bare majority. Trump publicly urged elimination of the filibuster to speed this agenda, framing it as necessary to secure the border and elections. The linkage was explicit. The stakes were high.

In the courts, the Republican National Committee pursued its own flank. It filed a lawsuit seeking stricter verification and counting rules for mail ballots, aiming to make it harder for such votes to be included. The Supreme Court agreed to review a challenge to Mississippi’s deadline for counting mail-in ballots that arrive after election day, a case with implications for close races and voter confidence. At the local level, a county sheriff in California seized and initiated recounts of more than 650,000 ballots from a prior election based on disputed fraud claims, blurring law-enforcement and electoral roles and risking public trust in neutral administration.

The executive branch prepared to go further still. Trump called for “nationalizing” aspects of voting, challenging the long-standing state-led structure of U.S. elections. A draft executive order under consideration would end machine and mail voting, require all voters to re-register with proof of citizenship, and mandate hand counts. Such an order would centralize sweeping changes to election rules in the presidency, bypassing legislatures and state officials. Civil-society groups like Democracy Docket tracked these moves and the related litigation, providing analysis that made the pattern visible: under the banner of “integrity,” the system was being reengineered to narrow the electorate and shift control of election machinery toward the executive and a partisan majority.

Immigration policy was another arena where lines between law, enforcement, and rights were redrawn. ICE and DHS expanded aggressive operations, including high-profile arrests at airports and intensified crackdowns in Minnesota. A legally documented Canadian mother and her child were detained in harsh conditions and pressured to self-deport. New rules tightened commercial driver’s license requirements for immigrants, stripping or threatening licenses for thousands of noncitizen truckers, including refugees, by imposing English and status conditions that many could not meet. These measures restricted access to work and mobility for disfavored groups.

Behind the scenes, ICE and Justice Department lawyers used false or misleading legal justifications to detain immigrants at courthouses. Internal memos were misrepresented to suggest broader authority for arrests than they actually conferred. A federal judge issued a preservation order for related communications, signaling concern about misuse of legal authority against people seeking lawful status. At the same time, advocates and detainees’ families testified before Congress about inhumane conditions at facilities like Stewart detention center, describing neglect and inadequate care for disabled detainees. The testimony gave human shape to what might otherwise have remained an abstract enforcement debate.

States, localities, and civil-rights groups responded with a wave of litigation. Michigan and the city of Romulus sued DHS over plans to convert a warehouse into a 500-bed detention center, raising environmental, procedural, and cooperative-governance objections. Minnesota and allied plaintiffs sued DOJ and DHS for withholding evidence in shootings by federal officers during “Operation Metro Surge,” seeking records needed to investigate potential misconduct. Class actions challenged detention and deportation of trafficking and domestic-violence survivors, alleging violations of the Trafficking Victims Protection Act. Individual suits, such as a Venezuelan immigrant’s claim of unconstitutional deportation and mistreatment, alleged systemic abuses in high-level enforcement decisions.

Courts provided important, if case-specific, protections. Judges blocked a policy to detain refugees lacking green cards, ordered the return of a deported DACA recipient, and temporarily halted immigrant license restrictions. A preliminary injunction in Minnesota required free, private phone access and expanded visitation for detainees, strengthening practical access to counsel. These rulings did not dismantle the enforcement apparatus, but they showed that legal protections for migrants, workers, and trafficking survivors still had force when brought before a judge. The result was a stratified citizenship regime contested in real time: harsher treatment for certain nationalities and statuses, checked at the margins by litigation and injunctions.

Law and security institutions more broadly were pulled toward partisan and ideological loyalty. Trump publicly demanded that the Attorney General pursue legal action against his political opponents, signaling an expectation that federal law enforcement serve presidential retribution rather than neutral justice. He labeled Democratic lawmakers’ comments about unlawful military orders as “seditious behavior, punishable by death,” recasting constitutional oversight as treason. The rhetoric raised the personal cost of dissent for elected officials and normalized the idea that opposition could be treated as a capital crime.

Personnel choices reinforced this tilt. The confirmation of Markwayne Mullin at DHS placed a loyalist in charge of a department central to immigration, election security, and domestic enforcement. At the Pentagon, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth overruled Army leaders to block promotions of four officers—two Black and two women—from a general-officer list, suggesting that ideological or demographic criteria now influenced advancement into the flag ranks. Hegseth also announced changes to the military chaplain corps, reducing religious affiliation codes while replacing rank insignia with religious symbols on uniforms, injecting explicit faith signaling into military structures. In public health, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention operated without a Senate-confirmed director, and a court voided an unlawfully appointed vaccine advisory panel, concentrating vaccine policy authority in a political appointee. The Senate’s stalled confirmation of a Surgeon General nominee left another key role unfilled.

Security vulnerabilities intersected with this politicization. A foreign-linked group hacked and published personal emails of FBI Director Kash Patel, exposing personal and work correspondence. The breach underscored how senior officials’ communications could be exploited in information operations at the very moment when the bureau’s neutrality was under question. In such an environment, the alignment of law enforcement and security forces with regime interests did not require formal decrees. It emerged from rhetoric, appointments, promotion decisions, and the selective pursuit or neglect of investigations.

Money and policy moved together in ways that blurred the line between governance and private gain. HealthEquity, a health-finance firm, made an unprecedented $1 million contribution to a Trump-aligned super PAC. Soon after, the administration expanded eligibility for Health Savings Accounts in ways that primarily benefited higher-income users, and the company advocated further changes to allow premium payments and higher contribution limits. The sequence illustrated how large donations could align with tax and health-policy shifts that favored donors, reinforcing a pay-to-play channel for corporate actors seeking bespoke regulatory outcomes.

In energy and climate policy, the administration paid nearly $1 billion to buy back offshore wind leases from TotalEnergies, steering the company toward U.S. oil and gas investment instead. The move redirected public funds from renewables to fossil fuels, privileging incumbent energy interests. California sued the Energy Department over its use of Defense Production Act authority to restart an offshore oil pipeline, arguing that the federal government was bypassing state law and court settlements under the guise of emergency economic powers. The case tested whether courts would check the use of national-security tools to advance industry goals.

Foreign financial ties deepened the entanglement of private and public interests. Saudi investments in Kushner’s firm and a Trump Organization project created direct economic links between a foreign monarchy and the president’s family businesses. At the same time, Saudi leaders lobbied for a more aggressive Iran campaign. Policy on war and regional alignment thus tracked the preferences of a government that was also a major investor in Trump-world. Executive orders added further layers: one restricted certain diversity, equity, and inclusion practices by federal contractors, chilling race-conscious equity programs in the private sector; another directed federal agencies to challenge state AI regulations seen as burdensome to innovation, asserting federal preemption in ways that weakened state-level protections against algorithmic discrimination and worker harms. State legislatures in Colorado and Texas adjusted their own AI discrimination laws, sometimes delaying or narrowing protections, while DHS immigration fee policies affected the ability of firms like Anthropic to recruit specialized workers. Across domains, business-aligned governance became the norm.

Information itself was a contested field. The White House used edited videos of military strikes as entertainment-style public messaging, packaging real combat footage as game-like content to promote the Iran war. Trump received war briefings as short highlight reels of successful strikes rather than full intelligence assessments, suggesting that internal information flows were curated to reinforce favorable narratives. He falsely announced negotiations with Iran that did not exist, coinciding with heavy trading in futures and massive swings in equities and oil prices. Suspicious prediction-market activity around ceasefire bets raised concerns that insiders might be monetizing privileged national-security information.

Institutional control over records and data tightened in selective ways. The FBI seized 700 boxes of 2020 election documents from Fulton County under a warrant whose supporting affidavit was alleged to contain misrepresentations, concentrating control of crucial electoral archives in federal hands. DOJ inadvertently disclosed an FBI memo about Trump’s classified documents to Congress, raising questions about how sensitive information was handled and who decided what lawmakers could see. In the Epstein case, a bipartisan law required DOJ to release files, and large disclosures followed, but a class action alleged that the department violated the Privacy Act by exposing survivors’ identities, while Google continued to index the unredacted records. The episode highlighted how transparency, victim protection, and data-handling practices could come into conflict.

Other agencies adjusted their data systems in quieter ways. EPA modified its acquisition records to allow sharing with Treasury for fraud detection, expanding inter-agency data flows with implications for privacy and oversight. It rescinded a grants management system as a Privacy Act system of records, changing how grant data were categorized and accessed. Notices of environmental impact statements for major projects maintained some transparency around high-impact decisions, even as other parts of the state grew more opaque. The CDC, under court order, canceled a key immunization advisory committee meeting, delaying expert guidance on vaccines and illustrating how litigation over advisory bodies could disrupt public-health information flows. At the same time, AI industry leaders emphasized existential risks and funded regulation and safety initiatives, shaping public and policymaker perceptions of the technology and steering regulatory agendas.

Beneath and around these moves, a struggle over national symbols and memory continued. Trump installed a reconstructed Christopher Columbus statue on White House grounds, resurrecting a monument destroyed during anti-racism protests and signaling an official endorsement of a contested figure. He announced architectural plans for central Washington—a massive ballroom, a grand arch, and the replacement of historic pavers with black granite—using control over the capital’s built environment to project a personalized aesthetic of grandeur. He decided that his signature would replace the treasurer’s on U.S. paper currency, embedding his name in a core national symbol that passes through every hand.

Rhetoric and ritual reinforced this personalization. Trump described Democrats as America’s “greatest enemy,” casting the opposition party as an existential threat rather than a legitimate alternative. The White House and House Speaker created and awarded a new “America First” prize to Trump at a party fundraiser, blurring lines between institutional leadership and personal loyalty ceremonies. At the same time, he celebrated the death of Robert Mueller on social media and attacked his legacy, sending a message that those who scrutinize presidential conduct could expect vilification even after their work ended. These choices curated memory: which figures were honored, which were vilified, and which stories were centered in the national narrative.

Yet the week also recorded counter-mobilization. Organizers prepared “No Kings” protests at more than 3,000 locations, a broad-based civic effort to oppose authoritarian drift and defend democratic norms. Courts and activists contested rights rollbacks in other arenas. A Georgia case in which a woman was charged with murder for using abortion pills under a heartbeat law drew judicial skepticism and minimal bail, illustrating both the harsh reach and contested legitimacy of new abortion regimes. A professor sued Texas State University, alleging his contract was terminated for off-campus political speech about Israel–Palestine, raising concerns about academic freedom. A class action over Epstein survivors’ privacy sought to enforce limits on how the state and platforms handle sensitive data. In North Carolina, a state board postponed action on a criticized voter-suppression bill after heavy public comment, showing that civic engagement could slow restrictive measures. The Army, facing recruitment pressures from ongoing conflicts, raised the maximum enlistment age and relaxed marijuana-related restrictions, modestly broadening access to a key public institution.

These acts of resistance did not reverse the week’s structural shifts, but they mattered for the clock. They absorbed some of the pressure generated by unilateral war-making, shutdown governance, voter restriction, and stratified citizenship. They kept certain lines from being crossed outright, or at least delayed their crossing. The result was a period in which the formal measure of democratic erosion did not move, even as the underlying contest over power, law, and memory intensified.

The week thus sits in the term’s larger arc as a moment of consolidation rather than rupture. Executive war powers were exercised as a matter of course. Emergency-style governance at home became a tool in ordinary policy fights. Law and security institutions bent further toward loyalty, while money and foreign influence threaded through health, energy, and Middle East decisions. At the same time, courts, states, and civil society showed that resistance remained possible, though often reactive and piecemeal. The equilibrium that kept the clock from advancing was fragile. It depended on institutions and citizens willing to bear higher costs to preserve boundaries that, in healthier times, would not have needed such defense.

This was an acute-crisis week in which an already fragile constitutional order was stressed on multiple fronts. The Iran war and related regional escalation dominated, with the president openly threatening strikes on civilian infrastructure, deploying and surging troops without authorization, and acknowledging a “military operation” in Iran absent congressional approval. That conduct, combined with Republicans’ refusal to exercise war oversight and massive off‑books war spending, drove severe pressure on executive constraint, separation of powers, and emergency normalization. Domestically, the DHS shutdown and ICE-at-airports experiment exposed how core public services can be held hostage to immigration and voter‑suppression demands, while TSA workers and other civil servants absorbed the costs. Parallel moves to advance the SAVE Act, data‑sharing of voter rolls with DHS, and even a draft executive order to effectively nationalize and constrict voting marked a coordinated attempt to reengineer electoral access under the banner of “integrity.” Law enforcement and courts were heavily politicized: selective prosecutions, settlements for Trump allies, aggressive ballot seizures, and FBI/ICE abuses contrasted with important but reactive judicial pushback. Symbolic personalization of the state—from Trump’s signature on currency to Columbus statuary and architectural remakes—reinforced a leader‑centric, revisionist narrative amid widening global and domestic instability.

Power and Authority

  1. Trump administration considered and prepared for major military escalation against Iran: Reports that the administration weighed an assault on Iran’s Kharg Island and prepared thousands of Marines for deployment signaled willingness to expand war-making without clear congressional authorization, concentrating life-and-death decisions in the executive branch. (2026-03-21)
  2. President Trump publicly threatened to bomb Iranian power and energy infrastructure if the Strait of Hormuz was not reopened: Trump’s ultimata to “obliterate” Iranian power plants to force reopening of the Strait of Hormuz showed the president personally directing potential strikes on civilian infrastructure, heightening risks of unlawful warfare and unchecked executive coercive power. (2026-03-22)
  3. President Trump announced and then extended pauses of planned bombing campaigns in Iran while claiming negotiations: Trump’s shifting announcements about pausing strikes for supposed talks with Iran, which Tehran denied, allowed him to move markets and shape public expectations about war from the bully pulpit without transparent process or oversight. (2026-03-23)
  4. President Trump acknowledged conducting a military operation in Iran without congressional approval: By describing the Iran campaign as a “military operation” and a success despite lacking war authorization, Trump normalized large-scale hostilities initiated solely by the executive, eroding Congress’s constitutional war powers. (2026-03-27)
  5. President Trump launched military strikes on Iran at the urging of foreign leaders despite no imminent threat finding: Initiating strikes on Iran based on lobbying from Saudi and Israeli leaders, rather than an imminent threat determination, highlighted susceptibility of U.S. war decisions to foreign influence and personal relationships over institutional checks. (2026-03-27)
  6. Pentagon deployed and prepared to deploy thousands of additional U.S. troops to the Middle East: Large new deployments of Army and Marine units to the Middle East deepened U.S. entanglement in the Iran conflict, committing substantial force structure under executive direction while Congress struggled to assert war-authorization authority. (2026-03-25)
  7. Pentagon considered diverting weapons and NATO funds from Ukraine to restock U.S. supplies for the Middle East: Plans to redirect weapons and $750 million in Ukraine-related NATO funding toward U.S. stockpiles for the Iran war showed the executive reshaping alliance commitments and battlefield priorities with limited public debate. (2026-03-27)
  8. President Trump eased long-standing sanctions on Iranian oil to influence global prices during the conflict: Lifting or waiving sanctions on Iranian oil during active hostilities gave the president unilateral leverage over a key adversary’s revenue and global energy markets, blending war policy with economic statecraft under centralized control. (2026-03-22)
  9. President Trump eased sanctions on Belarus to secure fertilizer imports amid the Hormuz crisis: Relaxing sanctions on Belarus to obtain fertilizer in response to the Hormuz closure showed the executive trading away human-rights leverage for short-term economic relief, with little visible legislative input. (2026-03-27)
  10. President Trump directed DHS by executive order to immediately pay TSA agents during the shutdown: Ordering DHS to pay TSA workers by executive fiat during a funding lapse underscored how the president can improvise around appropriations gridlock, both relieving hardship and normalizing ad hoc emergency governance. (2026-03-27)
  11. President Trump threatened to deploy ICE agents to airports and then ordered their deployment during the DHS shutdown: Using ICE agents in tactical gear to backfill unpaid TSA staff turned immigration enforcement into a visible political tool in civilian spaces, blurring lines between border policing and domestic security to pressure Congress. (2026-03-22)
  12. President Trump publicly demanded that the Attorney General pursue legal action against his political opponents: Pressuring the Attorney General to prosecute political adversaries signaled an expectation that federal law enforcement serve presidential retribution rather than neutral justice, undermining the separation between political power and prosecution. (2026-03-24)
  13. President Trump called Democratic lawmakers’ comments about unlawful military orders seditious and punishable by death: Labeling legislators’ criticism of potential illegal orders as “seditious behavior, punishable by death” framed constitutional oversight as treason, chilling dissent and signaling readiness to equate opposition with capital crimes. (2026-03-24)
  14. President Trump publicly urged elimination of the Senate filibuster to pass DHS funding and restrictive voting rules: Trump’s push to scrap the filibuster so Republicans could fund DHS and enact the SAVE America Act without Democrats highlighted his preference for majoritarian rule to entrench executive-aligned policy on security and voting. (2026-03-25)
  15. President Trump advocated for the SAVE America Act to impose strict proof-of-citizenship voting requirements and curb mail voting: By championing the SAVE America Act’s citizenship documentation and mail-vote limits, Trump used presidential influence to advance structural barriers to voting under the guise of fraud prevention. (2026-03-25)
  16. President Trump considered issuing an executive order to overhaul voting rules before the 2026 midterms: A draft executive order to end machine and mail voting, require re-registration with citizenship proof, and mandate hand counts would centralize sweeping changes to election administration in the presidency, bypassing normal legislative processes. (2026-03-27)
  17. President Trump called for nationalizing aspects of voting administration: Trump’s call to “nationalize” voting challenged the long-standing state-led structure of U.S. elections, raising the prospect of centralized executive influence over voter eligibility and procedures. (2026-03-24)
  18. President Trump publicly labeled the Democratic Party as America’s greatest enemy: Describing the opposition party as the country’s “greatest enemy” after launching military action abroad cast domestic rivals as existential threats, undermining norms that treat opposition as legitimate participants in governance. (2026-03-22)
  19. President Trump directed the Pentagon to divert weapons and missile-defense resources from Ukraine to the Iran theater: Reallocating weapons and funding away from Ukraine to support the Iran campaign allowed the executive to reshape U.S. security commitments and alliance priorities with limited public scrutiny. (2026-03-27)
  20. President Trump announced architectural and symbolic redesigns of central Washington, including large new structures and paving changes: Plans for a massive ballroom, arch, and replacement of historic pavers with black granite used presidential authority over the capital’s built environment to imprint a personalized aesthetic on national civic space. (2026-03-25)
  21. President Trump ordered continued operation of the FEMA Review Council by executive order: Extending the FEMA Review Council by executive order kept a presidentially controlled advisory body in place over disaster management, shaping how emergency policy recommendations reach the White House. (2026-03-24)
  22. President Trump issued an executive order restricting certain DEI practices by federal contractors: Barring contractors from engaging in DEI activities defined as racially discriminatory, with penalties including debarment, used federal contracting power to chill race-conscious equity programs in the private sector. (2026-03-26)
  23. President Trump issued an executive order directing federal agencies to challenge state AI regulations: Ordering Commerce and DOJ to identify and sue over state AI laws that allegedly burden innovation asserted federal preemption to weaken state-level protections against algorithmic discrimination and worker harms. (2026-03-26)
  24. President Trump announced that his signature would replace the treasurer’s on U.S. paper currency: Putting the sitting president’s signature on banknotes for the first time personalized a core national symbol, reinforcing leader-centric branding over institutional continuity. (2026-03-26)
  25. Governor Gavin Newsom signed an executive order banning insider betting by state officials on prediction markets: California’s ban on officials using nonpublic information to wager on prediction markets aimed to close a novel corruption channel, reinforcing ethical constraints on how public power can be monetized. (2026-03-27)

Institutions and Governance

  1. Republicans in Congress refused to exercise public oversight of the Iran war: By avoiding hearings and backing the president instead of scrutinizing his justification for war, Republican lawmakers weakened Congress’s checking role over large-scale military operations. (2026-03-21)
  2. Senate Democrats attempted to require congressional authorization for continued military operations in Iran: Democrats’ failed efforts to pass a war-authorization requirement highlighted both ongoing attempts to reassert legislative war powers and the structural difficulty of constraining unilateral executive action. (2026-03-21)
  3. Congress and the states (historical) enacted and ratified the Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments and intervened in Georgia’s legislature: The Civil War–era amendments and Congress’s refusal to seat Georgia legislators expelled for being Black established constitutional guarantees of equal protection and voting rights that remain central benchmarks for assessing current democratic backsliding. (1868-07-28)
  4. U.S. Supreme Court considered limiting the counting of mail-in ballots that arrive after election day: The Court’s review of an RNC challenge to Mississippi’s mail-ballot deadline could reshape when and how valid votes are counted, with implications for close races and voter confidence. (2026-03-23)
  5. Republican National Committee filed a lawsuit seeking stricter mail-ballot counting rules: The RNC’s suit to tighten verification and counting of mail ballots aimed to make it harder for such votes to be included, potentially disenfranchising lawful voters who rely on mail voting. (2026-03-23)
  6. State of California sued the U.S. Energy Department over restarting an offshore oil pipeline via Defense Production Act authority: California’s challenge to a DPA-based pipeline restart raised questions about federal agencies bypassing state law and court settlements, testing judicial checks on emergency economic powers. (2026-03-23)
  7. Multiple states and local governments filed lawsuits challenging Trump administration immigration and detention policies: New suits from Michigan, Minnesota, and others over detention centers, evidence withholding, and ICE operations showed states turning to courts to contest federal immigration practices they view as unlawful or opaque.   8. Federal courts issued multiple rulings adjusting the posture of challenges to Trump-era policies: Abeyance orders, TRO denials, clarifications, and stays in cases involving labor contracts, immigration, and DHS rules illustrated courts’ ongoing but often slow role in mediating disputes over executive actions. Federal judges blocked or limited several Trump administration immigration measures: Courts halted a refugee arrest policy, ordered the return of a deported DACA recipient, and temporarily blocked immigrant license restrictions, providing important, if case-specific, protections against overbroad enforcement.   10. Federal courts granted significant relief in cases challenging DHS and ICE practices affecting access to counsel and use of force: Injunctions requiring better phone and visitation access for detainees and litigation over tear gas near housing complexes showed courts enforcing due-process and safety norms against federal enforcement agencies. (2026-03-26)
  11. Federal courts issued key rulings in disputes over Anthropic’s access to government contracting: Temporary and preliminary injunctions against Pentagon bans on Anthropic’s AI tools suggested judicial skepticism of using supply-chain risk designations to punish companies for policy positions on autonomous weapons. (2026-03-26)
  12. State of Minnesota and allied plaintiffs sued DOJ and DHS for withholding evidence in shootings by federal officers: Minnesota’s suit to compel disclosure of records from “Operation Metro Surge” highlighted tensions between federal secrecy and state efforts to investigate potential misconduct by immigration agents. (2026-03-24)
  13. House committees held oversight hearings on DHS shutdown impacts, TSA staffing, and ICE detention conditions: Hearings documenting unpaid TSA workers, ICE transfers to airports, and poor detention conditions showed Congress using its investigative tools to surface the human and operational costs of executive and legislative stalemates. (2026-03-25)
  14. Senate Republicans and Democrats repeatedly failed to agree on DHS funding bills during a prolonged shutdown: Seven failed Senate votes and ongoing partisan disputes over ICE and voting provisions left DHS partially unfunded for weeks, degrading core security functions and illustrating legislative gridlock. (2026-03-27)
  15. House Republicans rejected a Senate-passed DHS funding package and pursued alternative plans: The House GOP’s refusal to take up a Senate compromise that excluded ICE funding prolonged the shutdown and underscored how one chamber’s majority can block restoration of basic government operations. (2026-03-27)
  16. Senate Republicans planned to use budget reconciliation to fund ICE and embed SAVE Act provisions: Exploring reconciliation to finance ICE and add voter ID rules would bypass the filibuster, using budget procedure to advance contentious enforcement and voting changes with a bare majority. (2026-03-25)
  17. Congress enacted a law authorizing the Medal of Honor for John W. Ripley: Awarding the Medal of Honor through statute reflected Congress’s ceremonial role in recognizing military valor and reinforcing norms of legislative participation in honoring service. (2026-03-26)
  18. Congress and President Trump mandated and implemented release of extensive Jeffrey Epstein-related DOJ records: A bipartisan law requiring DOJ to disclose Epstein files, and subsequent large releases, represented a rare instance of coordinated legislative-executive action to increase transparency in a politically sensitive case. (2025-11-19)
  19. House Oversight Committee deposed Jeffrey Epstein’s former lawyer and accountant about investigative gaps: Testimony that federal investigators never interviewed key Epstein associates raised questions about past prosecutorial decisions and the thoroughness of high-profile abuse investigations. (2026-03-25)
  20. Senate confirmed Markwayne Mullin as Secretary of Homeland Security: Confirming a Trump ally to lead DHS during a shutdown and immigration crackdown placed a loyalist atop a vast security bureaucracy, with implications for how neutrally the department enforces federal law. (2026-03-24)
  21. White House and House Speaker Mike Johnson created and awarded a new partisan 'America First' prize to Donald Trump: Establishing a symbolic award for Trump at a party fundraiser blurred lines between institutional leadership and personal loyalty rituals, reinforcing a leader-centric political culture. (2026-03-26)
  22. CDC and HHS left the CDC director position vacant while a court voided an unlawfully appointed vaccine panel: Operating the CDC without a Senate-confirmed director and relying on a health secretary whose advisory panel was ruled unlawful concentrated vaccine policy authority in a political appointee, weakening independent public-health governance. (2026-03-26)
  23. Senate stalled confirmation of Surgeon General nominee Casey Means: Extended inaction on a controversial Surgeon General nominee left a key public-health leadership role unfilled, limiting federal capacity to speak with authority on health issues during overlapping crises. (2026-03-26)
  24. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth blocked promotions of four Army officers, including Black and female candidates, from a general-officer list: Overruling Army leaders to remove two Black officers and two women from a promotion slate suggested ideological or demographic criteria influencing senior military advancement, politicizing the flag ranks. (2026-03-27)
  25. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced changes to the military chaplain corps emphasizing religious identity over rank: Reducing religious affiliation codes and replacing rank insignia with religious symbols on chaplains’ uniforms injected explicit faith signaling into military structures, raising church–state concerns. (2026-03-26)
  26. House and Senate members sought more information and briefings on Iran war strategy and costs: Lawmakers’ frustration over vague briefings and nearly $30 billion in war spending without clear objectives underscored how limited congressional insight into ongoing hostilities had become. (2026-03-25)
  27. Quebec National Assembly passed a motion calling for Air Canada’s CEO to resign over language used in a condolence message: The unanimous motion demanding a French-speaking CEO reflected a legislature asserting cultural and linguistic norms in corporate governance, illustrating how identity politics can shape institutional expectations. (2026-03-26)
  28. Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension and others voluntarily dismissed a federal suit against Governor Noem: Dropping a case against federal actors over criminal investigations signaled shifting litigation strategies in state–federal disputes about law-enforcement authority. (2026-03-24)
  29. Chicago Transit Authority won a TRO requiring DOT to resume processing major transit grants: A court order forcing the federal government to restart over $2 billion in transit grants after an allegedly arbitrary rule change showed judicial willingness to check selective enforcement of civil-rights-related funding rules. (2026-03-24)
  30. Eagle County, Colorado sued the Interior Department over expedited environmental review procedures for energy projects: Challenging a 14-day review process without public comment for certain energy projects tested whether executive streamlining can bypass statutory environmental safeguards and local input. (2026-03-26)
  31. House Judiciary Democrats received and scrutinized DOJ documents potentially violating a gag order in the Trump documents case: Jamie Raskin’s letter about DOJ disclosures that may have breached a court gag order highlighted tensions between congressional oversight, judicial control of evidence, and the handling of sensitive material involving the president. (2026-03-26)
  32. DHS Inspector General opened an investigation into DHS contracting practices involving Kristi Noem and Corey Lewandowski: An IG probe into potentially irregular DHS contracts signaled internal oversight mechanisms still functioning to examine favoritism or corruption in high-value federal procurement. (2026-03-27)
  33. Democracy Docket tracked and analyzed litigation affecting election rules and democratic access: Ongoing monitoring and analysis of voting-related cases by a specialized outlet provided civil-society infrastructure for understanding how court decisions reshape electoral rules. (2026-03-26)

Economic Structure

U.S. Treasury and Trump administration lifted or waived sanctions on Iranian oil already at sea: Allowing roughly 140 million barrels of Iranian oil to reach market to lower prices intertwined sanctions policy with short-term market management, potentially channeling funds to an adversary during war. (2026-03-21)
  3. HealthEquity and Trump administration combined a large corporate donation with regulatory expansion of Health Savings Accounts: HealthEquity’s unprecedented $1 million super PAC donation and subsequent HSA eligibility expansions primarily benefiting higher-income users illustrated how campaign money can align with tax and health-policy changes favoring donors. (2026-03-23)
  4. Trump administration paid TotalEnergies nearly $1 billion to buy back offshore wind leases: Spending $928 million to cancel wind projects and steer the company toward U.S. oil and gas investment redirected public funds from renewables to fossil fuels, privileging incumbent energy interests. (2026-03-25)
  5. Saudi Public Investment Fund and Trump family businesses channeled billions into Jared Kushner’s firm and a Trump Organization project: Saudi investments in Kushner’s fund and a Trump-branded development created deep financial ties between a foreign monarchy and the president’s family enterprises, raising conflict-of-interest concerns around Middle East policy. (2026-03-25)

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman lobbied President Trump to continue and expand the war against Iran: MBS’s push for regime-change-oriented strikes on Iran, coinciding with major Saudi financial ties to Trump-world, highlighted how foreign and private interests can shape costly U.S. military commitments. (2026-03-25)

Financial markets and Polymarket users showed suspicious trading patterns around Iran ceasefire bets and Trump announcements: Unusual prediction-market activity and massive swings in equities and oil prices around Trump’s Iran statements raised concerns that insiders might be monetizing privileged national-security information.   9. Iranian government closed the Strait of Hormuz and imposed tolls affecting global energy shipments: Iran’s closure and tolling of the Strait of Hormuz disrupted a key route for global oil and LNG, triggering fuel shortages and emergency measures abroad and demonstrating how chokepoints can be weaponized economically. (2026-03-25)
  10. Asian governments implemented emergency work and education measures to conserve fuel: Work-from-home orders, shortened workweeks, and early university closures in Asia illustrated how distant conflicts can force abrupt changes in domestic economic and social routines. (2026-03-25)
  11. U.S. Postal Service responded to Middle East conflict by planning fuel surcharges on domestic shipping: USPS’s planned surcharge on packages due to war-related fuel costs highlighted how geopolitical instability can erode the affordability of essential public services. (2026-03-26)
  12. HealthEquity advocated for further expansion of HSA rules that primarily benefit higher earners: Proposals to broaden HSA eligibility, allow premium payments, and raise contribution limits would deepen tax advantages for wealthier households, reinforcing inequality in health financing. (2026-03-23)
  13. EPA and other federal regulators issued multiple environmental and chemical regulatory decisions and settlements: Approvals of state air plans, hazardous-waste program revisions, chemical findings, and Superfund settlements showed routine but consequential regulatory work shaping environmental quality and corporate liability.   14. FDA and CDC advanced or adjusted multiple health-related regulatory processes and data collections: Hearings, information-collection notices, device reclassifications, and survey approvals reflected ongoing technocratic governance of drug, device, and health-data policy that underpins public health and industry operations. (2026-03-23)

  21. AI industry leaders and firms publicly emphasized existential AI risks and funded regulation and safety initiatives: Statements by Anthropic, Elon Musk, and OpenAI about catastrophic AI risks, alongside lobbying and funding for risk-prevention foundations, signaled industry support for stronger AI governance frameworks. (2026-03-26)
  22. Colorado and Texas legislatures adjusted state AI discrimination laws affecting workers’ rights: Colorado’s delay of its AI discrimination law and Texas’s narrower Responsible AI Governance Act showed states experimenting with, and sometimes weakening, protections against algorithmic bias in employment. (2026-03-26)
  23. (2026-03-27)
  24. Anthropic and other plaintiffs reported DHS denials of H-1B fee exemptions and sought court review: DHS’s refusal to grant H-1B fee exemptions, allegedly mischaracterizing requests, highlighted how immigration fee policies can affect labor markets and the ability of organizations to recruit specialized workers. (2026-03-26)

Information, Memory and Manipulation

  1. White House used edited videos of military strikes as entertainment-style public messaging: Packaging real combat footage as game-like content to promote the Iran war risked normalizing violence and shaping public opinion through spectacle rather than sober information. (2026-03-20)
  2. President Trump celebrated the death of Robert Mueller and attacked his legacy on social media: Trump’s gloating posts about Mueller’s death vilified a former investigator and signaled that those who scrutinize presidential conduct can expect ongoing public smears even after leaving office.
